subject: 5+ unit small multi-family: the under-priced sweet spot
preheader: Commercial pricing kicks in at 5+ · cap-rate compression upside · the under-management opportunity

marketSnapshot.headline: 5-12 units sits in a different math zone
marketSnapshot.body: Single-family and 2-4 unit properties are 'residential' for financing purposes. At 5+ units the property becomes 'commercial' — different loan products, different appraisal methodology, different exit dynamics. Small multi-family in the 5-12 unit range is an interesting sweet spot: still affordable enough for individual investors ($500k-1.5M), big enough to have economies of scale on management, and priced primarily on NOI which means operational improvements directly compound the property value.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 8.2% cap · NOI improvements compound exit value
dealSpotter.body: $725k 6-unit. Commercial-style loan at 25-30% down. The math advantage of small multi: commercial buyers price these on cap rate compression. Strong NOI improvements (raise rents 5%, install coin-op laundry, sub-meter utilities) directly compound the exit value. A 100bp cap-rate compression on an 8% cap property is roughly $90k of value creation.

$1.05M 8-unit in a gentrifying neighborhood. Long-time owner has under-rented vs market for years. The opportunity isn't the headline cap rate (which is OK, not great) — it's the documented gap between current rents and market rents. Closing that gap over 3-4 years through natural turnover unlocks meaningful NOI growth that compounds in the exit value.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 4 units strong · 1 tenant-from-hell is the whole deal
dealSpotter.body: $485k 5-unit. Four units well-tenanted at market rents. The 5th has a long-term tenant paying significantly below market that the owner has been afraid to evict. Honest assessment: that unit's tenant IS the deal. If you can negotiate a cash-for-keys arrangement ($3-5k) or wait out the lease, you unlock substantial monthly upside that's worth $100k+ in exit value. If they won't move, you've inherited the problem.

blogFeature.title: DSCR loans explained: rates, requirements, and when they make sense
blogFeature.excerpt: Small multi-family financing often runs through commercial lenders rather than DSCR. But for 5-10 unit deals where DTI doesn't clear conventional, DSCR is sometimes the right structure.

qa.question: Is 5-12 units actually a better entry point than building up from single-family?
qa.answer: Depends on starting point. The case for going straight to small multi-family: economies of scale on management (one PM relationship for 8 units vs eight relationships for 8 SFRs), value-add upside on under-managed properties, and commercial pricing on cap-rate compression. The case against: bigger capital requirement ($200-400k down on a $1M deal), commercial financing is harder for first-timers without W-2 income or property-management track record, and the asset class has different operational rhythms (commercial lenders want a property-management background or hire a credentialed PM). Practical answer: most investors should do 1-3 SFRs first to learn the operational side, then jump to small multi-family. The smaller-scale learning curve on a $200k SFR is less painful than on a $1M 6-unit.
